items.text: Speculative Design · Design Research · Interaction Design
Exploring how different modes of expression shape collaboration, and imagining more inclusive ways of learning together at NID in 2030.

items.text:
Our initial assumptions about the future of learning were grounded in lived experience and speculative brainstorming. To validate and expand on these intuitions, we conducted a targeted literature review of global reports, educational research and foresight documents. 
Studies revealed recurring patterns:

children.text: Due to AI-based learning tools and constant feedback loops.
A rise in introversion, identity fatigue and digital loneliness
In an increasingly mediated campus culture.
A need for reflective, low-stimulation environments

items.text: These insights helped us validate our assumptions and build a futures-oriented framework, TESEEC, to map the key forces shaping design education at NID in 2030.
Sources referred: Harvard Business School, Pew Research Center, UNESCO, OECD, Stanford HAI and the World Economic Forum.
We adapted the PESTEL approach to the context of design education, developing TESEEC as a way to organise the forces that could shape learning at NID in 2030.

children.text: AI-driven personalization, datafication, and emotional surveillance redefining how students learn and are assessed.
Persistent “quiet bias” and the need for inclusive, reflective learning models that value varied expressions of engagement.
Cognitive overload and overstimulation, calling for hybrid and sensory-balanced studio environments.
Shifting peer dynamics, digital isolation, and the erosion of spontaneous community among students.
Platformization and privatization of learning, deepening inequalities in educational access and autonomy.
Changing norms of expression and identity, revaluing introspection, and authenticity as valid modes of participation.

items.text: The Semantic Differential Scale framed expression as a learning spectrum. Seven axes were used to construct the survey, with reflective and expressive attributes positioned at opposite ends.

children.text: Affects engagement rhythm, burnout, and recovery after critique.

Helps understand spatial design needs for inclusivity.

Ties to confidence, presentation, and classroom equity.
Gets at the “visibility bias” in design education.

items.text: Grey: the reflective and expressive ends of each axis (the first of its two questions). A version you can try yourself is coming.

The survey responses were developed into seven learner archetypes. These are best understood as patterns in how people may express themselves and engage with learning, rather than fixed personality categories.

items.text: Directed storytelling was then used to explore how students actually experience learning, belonging and collaboration at NID. Rather than relying only on direct questions, participants were encouraged to narrate personal experiences.
The interviews moved through six themes:

children.text: First encounters, early coping, social initiation.
Personal learning rhythm, autonomy, reflection, sensory needs.
Team dynamics, conflict, validation, emotional labour.
If NID were reimagined for you
Future-facing imagination, role of tech, ideal systems.

items.text: The conversations were translated into empathy maps to organise what participants said, did, thought and felt. Recurring themes included overwhelm and difficulty finding a starting point; community, mentorship and social validation; the need for structure and actionable goals; creative block; feedback and peer review; and time constraints and focus.

Observations were grouped through affinity mapping to identify recurring patterns across participants: overwhelm and the need for structure, actionable starting points, community and validation, practical application and project completion, and control and flexibility.

A causal map then connected these barriers to underlying needs: structured paths, feedback and validation, practical application and flexibility. The key tension it showed was personalization versus infrastructure: the system must be built with a flexible infrastructure, because rigidity is perceived as a barrier to personalized, comfortable learning.

children.text: Students move between reflection and articulation depending on context, confidence and emotional safety.
Visibility is not the same as participation.
Making, writing and observation can be meaningful contributions, even when they are not immediately visible.
Students may contribute in different ways, such as structuring, organising or freely generating ideas.
Students have different preferences for when and how they receive feedback.
Silence may indicate reflection or observation rather than disengagement.
Environments and tools should accommodate different paces and interaction styles.

items.text: How do we make learning more collaborative for individuals with different levels of expression at NID in 2030?

Bodystorming and roleplaying helped bring possible situations into an acted, embodied setting. How Might We mapping reframed research findings as opportunities for design. Wizard of Oz testing allowed us to simulate an intelligent system before building one.

The initial ideation produced twelve directions, ranging from algorithmic group formation and collaboration platforms to mentor selection, self-reflection tools, scenario-based games, wearables, spatial partitions and AI support.

items.text: Concepts were selected on the basis of plausibility, potential impact, and room for experimentation. Three directions were developed further: NID Commons, the Empathy Game and the AI Energy Flow Mediator.

items.text: NID Commons explored how a digital platform could support student collaboration. The first prototype used learner profiles and a compatibility matrix to suggest groups.

children.text: An algorithmic compatibility matrix formed balanced teams. It visualised learner diversity, but failed to sustain engagement among reflective participants.

The SMART Goals framework (goals that are Specific, Measurable, Achievable, Relevant and Time-bound) improved clarity, accountability and participation balance, yet collaboration still depended on user initiative.
Combined digital collaboration, adaptive campus mapping and reflective interaction tools, with a simpler, more inclusive user flow.

items.text: The platform offered ways to organise collaboration, but still depended on students arriving with an existing purpose. It exposed a gap between providing infrastructure for collaboration and helping people initiate it.

items.text: Rather than only discussing different communication styles, players had to experience the effects of communication, interpretation and coordination while working towards a common goal.
Players had to describe information without revealing a hidden goal pattern, infer the pattern from cues and actions, and coordinate the timing of their contributions.

children.text: Teams could lose when communication broke down.
A dominant player could complete the task while limiting meaningful collaboration.
Players could coordinate through strategic communication, specialised roles and shared understanding.

items.text: Completing the task did not necessarily mean the team had collaborated well.
A playable version of the game will live here.
The AI Energy Flow Mediator explored how an AI-based companion could support group work through conversational guidance and adaptive lighting.
The final Wizard of Oz test used a mock interface operated by human facilitators behind the scenes.

children.text: students with varied learner archetypes took part in the test

items.text: Reflective learners appreciated the non-judgmental text dialogue, while expressive learners valued quick motivational feedback. The test also raised concerns about overreliance on automated empathy.
The exploration suggested that AI could supplement human mentorship, but should not replace it.

items.text: The project made me more comfortable working with ambiguity. Rather than trying to predict what NID might look like in 2030, we used speculative design to explore possibilities and ask better questions. It also made me think differently about collaboration: participation is not always loud or visible, and productive disagreement can be just as important as compatibility.
